Thank you very much, Madam Chair, ladies and gentlemen. Distinguished delegates, I'm pleased to outline to you the main interests and developments in the Tunisian space sector. Based on our prestigious history in this area, our human capacity, as well as our agricultural heritage, our favorable geographic location has allowed us to strengthen our position in the space sector, catalyzing international development and cooperation through the peaceful application and uses in order to attain the SDGs. In the context of our national strategy, the space sector has acquired increasing importance regarding its use by public authorities, academia, and the private sector. As such, Tunisian youth is building further initiatives in order to gain access to this area. When it comes to space technology, we are particularly interested in scientific development. Such as the launch of small satellites and GNSS applications, the development of satellite reception networks, and integrating artificial intelligence in numerous areas. Currently, a significant quantity of data is provided through space technology in order to to find tangible solutions to tackle emerging challenges such as Earth observation, data analysis. The relevant ministries, academia, as well as companies are making use of space imagery in order to integrate artificial intelligence systems in order to develop smart agriculture, to combat desertification in arid areas, and to study soil specificities for the purpose of water resource management. This is particularly relevant as in so doing this will guarantee food security and allow us to mitigate climate change. Moreover, the National Land Mapping and Remote Sensing Center in Tunisia also provides and makes use of space imagery and data in order to help quantify and qualify development. The same applies to coastal erosion strategies, studying maritime pollution, and ensuring follow-up and monitoring of sea levels, which are all particularly relevant when it comes to the protection of Tunisia's coasts. The National Meteorological Institute also makes use of space data, which is particularly relevant in order to take stock of climate change developments such as floodings, droughts, earthquakes, and climate change. In order to further build the space sector capacity in a comprehensive fashion, we are working towards establishing a regulatory framework that is conducive to that purpose in order to harness the use of the space sector. We have also enacted new space legislation to attract investment, build innovation, and foster cooperation among the various national authorities and international partners. In order to enhance resources, international cooperation plays a vital role in order to help strengthen the sector, and we hope to build closer partnerships with international associations as well as with the private sector in order to take on board cutting-edge technology and benefit from international expertise. Equally, the Tunisian authorities believe that the space sector provides opportunities for sustainable development through investing in research and development, providing training, and raising awareness. Accordingly, we have organized annual scientific encounters in Tunisia in order to help build our capacity and allow us to participate in the space sector. We fully believe that as a result of the efforts made by all parties involved, and in particular in the context of activities under the aegis of the United Nations Office of Outer Space Affairs, UNOSA, Tunisia will be able to harness these various opportunities provided through the space sector so that in turn these can serve as catalysts in support of good governance and in support of our citizens and to resolve challenges related to the space sector and the climate worldwide.

Thank you, distinguished chair. Your Excellencies, distinguished delegates, it is an honor to address this subcommittee on behalf of the World Space Week Association. We extend our sincere gratitude to the chair, the secretariat, and the director of the United Nations Office for Outer Space Affairs. For their tireless efforts in convening this important session. World Space Week, proclaimed by the United Nations General Assembly in 1999, is celebrated annually from October 4th to 10th. As the largest global space-themed event, it provides a unique platform to bridge space activities and societal impact. Fostering public engagement with space activities and their benefits for humanity. This initiative invites member states to showcase achievements, promote awareness, and inspire innovation within their communities through the annual celebration of World Space Week. By participating, countries not only amplify their contributions to the space sector, but also strengthen global cooperation, and public understanding of the role of space in addressing shared challenges. In 2024, World Space Week celebrated its 25th anniversary under the theme Space and Climate Change. This theme underscored the critical role of space technologies in addressing one of humanity's most pressing issues. From satellite monitoring of environmental changes to enabling disaster response and climate resilience, space provides invaluable tools to mitigate the impacts of climate change. We were honored to have Peter Platzer, Executive Chairman of Spire Global, as our honorary chair. Spire Global's work in satellite-powered climate solutions set the tone for a year of impactful activities. Throughout 2024, the association facilitated global participation through public outreach campaigns, educational initiatives, and resources available at our website, www.worldspaceweek.org. A significant milestone in 2024 was the launch of the STEM Educators for Climate Awards. Recognizing teachers globally for their efforts in advancing education on space and climate change. This initiative not only celebrated the contributions of educators, but also emphasized the importance of nurturing future leaders equipped to address climate challenges through space innovation. With over 15,000 events held in over 80 countries, 2024 saw outstanding engagement. Pakistan recorded the highest number of events, followed very closely by Saudi Arabia, Ireland, Croatia, Romania, and Turkey, showcasing the diverse global enthusiasm for World Space Week. As we turn to the future, the theme for World Space Week 2025 is Living in Space and will highlight the growing reality of sustained human presence beyond Earth. This theme seeks to explore the development of innovative technologies, sustainable solutions, and international collaboration essential for long-term habitation in space. We are delighted to announce Robert Lightfoot, President of Lockheed Martin Space, as the Honorary Chair for 2025. With his extensive expertise and leadership in space exploration and development, Mr. Lightfoot will guide efforts to inspire and prepare global audiences for the exciting possibilities of living and thriving in space. World Space Week serves as a unifying platform for celebrating achievements, sharing innovations, and fostering dialogue about the future of space exploration. We invite the subcommittee, its member states, and permanent observers to embrace World Space Week 2025 as an opportunity to showcase your accomplishments, engage engage your communities and contribute to a global narrative of exploration and innovation. We are very grateful to our board, national coordinators, event holders, and sponsors including SPIRE Global, Lockheed Martin, Airbus, Viasat, Eutelsat, VAST, Kuwait Investment Company, and SLU, and many others whose support has been instrumental in the success of this initiative. Their contributions enable us to sustain and expand and the impact of World Space Week year after year. Thank you, distinguished chair and esteemed delegates, for your attention and continued support. Together we can continue to build bridges between space and society, one celebration at a time. Thank you.

The International Academy of Astronautics has played a significant role in promoting international cooperation and advancing the field of astronautics since its establishment in 1960. Recognized by the United Nations in 1996, the Academy operates as an independent non-governmental organization with a mission to bring together eminent experts in astronautics for the betterment of humanity. With approximately 1,100 members and corresponding members from 94 countries, The Academy boasts a diverse and distinguished membership base. Members are individuals who have made significant contributions to astronautics and related scientific fields, and their election to the Academy is a recognition of their achievements and services. The Academy engages in various scientific activities aimed at fostering international cooperation and advancing knowledge in astronautics. This includes organizing conferences, symposia, and meeting— meetings covering a wide range of topics such as space sciences, technology development, policy, and their impacts on society. These events provide platforms for discussing key issues in astronautics, sharing research findings, and fostering collaboration among professionals. During 2024, the number of IAME regional meetings and standalone conferences amounted to 23. The Academy is publishing the journal Acta Astronautica, which reached in 2023 an impact factor of 3.52. More than 1 million downloads were counted of this publication were counted in 2022. The Academy also publishes cosmic studies journals, dictionaries in multiple languages, and book series on relevant subjects. More than 75 cosmic studies are available on the IAA website, iaa.space.org. In 2024, the Academy contributed significantly to the International Astronautic local Congress, preparing a substantial portion of the program. More than 67 sessions brought the Academy contribution to the Congress to 35% of the entire event. During 2025, the Academy will organize more than 20 conferences, and we would like to mention here some conferences coming this spring, such as the 11th Space Traffic Management Conference in Austin, Texas, in March; the 9th Planetary Defense Conference in Stellenbosch, South Africa, in May; the 15th Symposium on Small Satellites for Earth System Observation in May in Berlin, Germany; and the 12th Symposium on the Future of Space Exploration in May in Turin, Italy. The Academy, through its committees, commissions, and study groups, is covering all substantive agenda items of the Subscientific and Technical Subcommittee agenda, contributing to the global extension and continuity of knowledge development in the space and space-related areas. For this session, I would like to mention the contribution of the Academy to the initiative to the protection of dark and quiet skies, and to the need for the designation and preservation of sites of special interest on the Moon. This approach enables the participation of experts from non-spacefaring spacefaring countries, offering them opportunities to engage in space activities, uh, and potentially initiate space program in their own region. Overall, the academy play— continues to play a vital role in advancing astronautics, fostering international cooperation, and promoting the peaceful exploration and utilization of space for the benefit of humanity. You can be assured, Madam Chair, that the International Academy of Astronautics will remain proactive in contributing to the goals and program— programs that make the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space a very unique body for the benefit of all nations. I thank you for your attention.

Thank you, Madam Chair. Madam Chair, to achieve long-term sustainability of outer space activities, we need a comprehensive and holistic approach. One critical element of LTS shall be the consideration of the challenges posed by space debris, particularly for emerging spacefaring nations that face heightened risks due to financial and technological constraints. The rapid expansion of space activities has led to an increase in space debris, which disproportionately affects countries still in, in the process of developing their space program. While developed nations have historically contributed to the majority of space debris, it is developing countries, often lacking adequate resources and mitigation capabilities, that may bear the burden. The risk of collisions with debris threatens not only their satellites but also the continuity and viability of their space programs. To address this inequity and ensure the sustainability of space activities, The Islamic Republic of Iran recommends that COPUS and its subcommittees consider the establishment of a fund to support developing countries that experience damages to the satellite due to the space debris. And we are happy to hear that there are other delegations, including the Egyptian delegation, who presented this idea, and we are happy to see that this idea is getting this broader support. In this body. This fund would provide essential assistance to emerging spacefaring countries in mitigating the consequences of debris-related incidents. The support offered by this fund could take multiple forms, including financial assistance for the repair or replacement of damaged satellites, capability-building initiatives such as training programs, technical workshops, and research grant enhanced capabilities of developing countries in managing space debris risk and cooperation mechanism to facilitate access to advanced debris mitigation technologies and enhance the capabilities of the satellites in order not to be easily turned to be debris. Such an initiative would not only alleviate the immediate impact of space debris but also contribute to the long-term stability and inclusivity of space activities. By ensuring that develop— by ensuring that developing nations remain active participants in the global space community, we can foster a more equitable and cooperative space environment. Moreover, the establishment of this fund would reinforce the principle of space equity, aligning with international commitments such as the Outer Space Treaty, which underscored the importance of cooperation in the peaceful use of outer space. By supporting this initiative, member states, particularly those with advanced space capabilities, can demonstrate their commitment to a just and sustainable future in space where all nations can pursue their space ambiguities— ambitious, sorry, their space ambitions without undue hardship. This proposal differs from the Convention on International Liability for Damage Caused by Space Objects, or Liability Convention. The Liability Convention establishes a framework for holding a launching state liable for damage caused by its space objects, including compensation claims for harm inflicted on other states. However, it does not comprehensively address the cumulative and long-term risks posed by space debris. Which often result from decades of space debris rather than a single identifiable launching state. This proposal advocates for proactive and collective approach by establishing a dedicated fund to assist developing countries affected by space debris, regardless of whether the responsible entity can be identified. The Islamic Republic of Iran considers this proposal as a step toward ensuring that all countries, regardless of their level of development, can access and benefit from space activities without being disproportionately affected by consequences of past space endeavors. While I have the floor, if you allow me, Madam Chair, I would like to address the proposal by UAE. I think and we believe this proposal is a very important proposal. We have a we received some instructions saying that we have seen some opportunities and at the same time challenges in this specific important issue. A more strategic and informed approach is needed to ensure that any future mechanism is well integrated and serve its intended purposes while we are focusing on the role of the corpus that should not be undermined. Thank you, Madam Chair.

Distinguished guests, salaam alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. My name is Ali Al Hammadi, CEO of Farman. An Emirati startup that combines satellite data and imagery, AI, and remote sensing to provide actionable insight for smart cities and environmental monitoring. It's an honor to be here today representing Farmen under the oversight of the UAE Space Agency to discuss how space-based technologies are transforming environmental monitoring and geospatial intelligence. As Foreman, we are fortunate to work closely with the UAE Space Agency, who leads several strategic space programs. Among them, the Space Analytics and Solutions Program, SAS, is the one we are most aligned with. The SAS program provides access to funding, satellite imagery, and technical support. Using our technical expertise, we can transform them into actionable insights. Now, it goes without saying how space technologies has been transformational in saving our environment. And I'm here today because I believe we all share a common concern for the future of our planet. The global warming continues to challenge us, and 2 major culprits, methane and carbon dioxide, are the ones to blame.

And the good news is that we have the tools to address this.

Now, we often hear about carbon dioxide, but we often less hear about its younger brother, methane. Like any younger brother, it's more dangerous. In fact, methane is 85 times more potent over a 20-year period. Yet detecting and tracking these gases is no easy feat. Traditional methods are expensive, slow, and don't always provide the full picture. Many systems rely on estimates and often lag behind reality, which is why accurate and timely data is so crucial. Now, imagine a system that not only captures the broad picture but also allows us to zoom in with pinpoint accuracy. In collaboration with the UAE Space Data Center, we have developed a multi-tiered approach, leveraging satellite data to track emissions at different levels. Country levels is the first level. And at this level, we are tracking overall trends, mapping out regions of concern, and observing the impact of national policies. We can highlight shifts in emissions across entire countries. We then narrow our focus to urban areas. This is crucial for identifying hotspots, those industrial and residential areas where emissions over 10,000 kilograms are having the biggest impact. Cities are often the key to driving change, and this level of detail supports targeted local policy. Zooming even further, we monitor specific sites like factories, power plants, and landfills, capturing emissions as small as 1,000 kilograms per hour. This allows for site-specific intervention and more granular understanding of sources. All of these are already rolled out. We are now working on the final, most refined analysis Which is our source level, which will allow us to detect emissions as low as 100 kilograms per hour. Whether it is a small industrial leak or minor agricultural source, we can pinpoint it, track it, and help mitigate it quickly. And here is the best part. Much of this is based on open-source data, making it both scalable and accessible. This means we are breaking down barriers to comprehensive GHG monitoring. Now, how does it work? How do we actually detect these gases from space? It's all about wavelength absorption. Now imagine a banana. It looks yellow because it absorbs all other colors and reflects only yellow. Methane and carbon dioxide similarly have unique colors, or what we call spectral signature, that we can detect using satellite imagery. Of course, water can absorb many of these wavelengths, as we can see here from the graph, which makes offshore detection quite tricky. But we have developed ways to minimize interferences and focus on accurate measurements. Our model starts with reliable local data and leverages global datasets. We factor in population density, vegetation, and industrial activities. As well as other relevant regional factors such as meteorological variables, wind, dust, and humidity, all critical components to ensure the accuracy of our detections. Our system is validated with over 90% accuracy across different scales and regions. We are confident that our approach is both effective and reliable, providing accurate data that stakeholders can act upon. Here is a visual example, the Arabian Peninsula. Over the years, we have monitored increasing level of methane and CO2, and it's clear we can see more yellow over the years, which means more emission. This regional data allows us to track long-term trends and evaluate the effectiveness of international policies. If we zoom in, We look at specific cities, industrial zones, and higher-density residential areas, which tend to show higher concentrations, as we can see in the examples here in Dubai and Qatar. This detailed analysis empowers urban planners to focus mitigation efforts where they will have greater impact, saving both time and resources. Now, of course, we can go even further to site level. Here is a case study of a refinery we monitored. We can see the usual methane, but here is a sudden spike in methane emission, a probable leak. Thanks to continuous observation and the work on the, on the ground, we tracked the anomaly, allowing for a quick intervention. Which we are thankful for them. This targeted approach not only addresses the immediate problem, but provides long-term insight to prevent future incidents. So why are we discussing this here today, and how is this related for global space governance? One, cost-effectiveness and scalability. Satellites provide affordable near real-time monitoring compared to ground-based inspection and drone inspections. Second, customizable detection levels from global to site-specific precision. Third, early detection, reducing response time and economic losses through this methodology. Fourth, predictive analytics. We can anticipate and mitigate future emission spikes based on trends. And of course, most importantly, because of the policy and support, government can shape stronger environmental policy using real data and actionable data. Now, all of this is great because it can allow us to go on a global impact. In fact, by a study of IEA, if we can reduce 75% of methane leaks, which is possible through this technology, we can cut up to 60 million metric tons of methane emissions and CO2 equivalent, which is equivalent to $5 billion in savings. By leveraging space-based GHG monitoring, we can turn data into action, enabling a cleaner, faster, and more sustainable future. Thank you a lot for having me here today and for your time. Sustainable Space Exploration: Integrating Culture, Commerce, and Collaboration. I'm Chantal Byer, and I sit as a board of director and represent the National Space Society. Distinguished delegates, esteemed colleagues, and honored guests, it is a privilege to stand before you today as we discuss one of the most critical frontiers of our time, sustainable space exploration. As humanity expands beyond Earth, we face an urgent question: how can we ensure that our pursuit of the universe does not repeat these mistakes of our past, but instead builds a future of balance, inclusivity, and responsibility. Sustainability in space is not just an environmental imperative; it is an economic necessity, a cultural opportunity, and a moral obligation. We must create a future where economic growth, environmental preservation, and cultural inclusion coexist. Not only on Earth, but beyond. Today, we define sustainability in space. We must look beyond short-term missions and resource extraction. A truly sustainable space economy must minimize environmental harm, preventing debris, limiting ecological impact, And ensuring responsible resource utilization. We must foster economic longevity, building business models that prioritize long-term ecological and financial viability. We must honor cultural heritage, ensuring that space remains a domain for all of humanity, reflecting our shared history and aspirations. We are not merely exploring space. As we explore space, we are shaping a new civilization beyond Earth. As we do, we must ask, what legacy will we leave? Sustainability is not just about survival. It is about identity, heritage, and meaning. Throughout history, culture and creativity have defined civilizations. Space should be no different. Imagine a future where art, literature, and design inspire responsible space exploration. From Jeff Koons' moon phase sculptures to installations that remind us of our shared humanity that exist on the Moon today, commemorating 125 historical figures that connect us to the Moon. Cultural artifacts such as that music and narratives accompanying missions, that we ensure expansion does not lose touch with what makes us human. Diverse voices shape space policies and missions, from Indigenous wisdom on resource stewardship to contemporary artists imagining futures beyond consumption-driven Expansion. If we treat space as nothing more than a resource, we reduce its potential. But if we integrate culture and creativity, we unlock a new kind of sustainability, one that preserves both nature and human spirit. While commerce is often seen as a driver of exploitation, It can also be a force for good if built with sustainability in mind. For instance, we have satellite mega constellations that must be designed with deorbiting mechanisms to prevent dangerous orbital debris. We have resource utilization on the moon and asteroids that must prioritize minimal impact, much like the principles of sustainable mining on Earth. Business models must shift from extraction to regeneration, ensuring that every commercial venture contributes positively to the space environment. We have this opportunity to set a new economic precedent, one where profit and planet are not at odds but mutually reinforcing. History has taught us what happens when development outpaces responsibility. We have seen environmental degradation, resource depletion, and economic short-termism drive unsustainable practices on Earth. We cannot afford to replicate these mistakes in space. We need to look at renewable energy initiatives We can develop closed-loop systems for energy generation on the Moon and Mars. Let's look at our circular economies. We can ensure that material use in space is, is repurposed and reused. Conservation strategies. We can designate protected zones in space for science research and cultural heritage. Sustainability is not the responsibility of one nation or one company. It's a global endeavor. To ensure our collective future is secured, we must establish international guidelines for responsible resource use. We must foster public-private partnerships to integrate sustainability into commercial space We must promote cross-disciplinary collaboration between governments, industry, artists, and environmentalists to create a holistic approach to space exploration. Only through unity can we shape a future where commerce, culture, and conservation work in harmony. Innovation will define the next phase of sustainable space exploration. When we apply creativity to sustainability, we not only solve problems, we inspire solutions.
